title: Designing Interactions
author: Bill Moggridge
note: Selected for named design specialists' praise and Goodreads 3.98/2,456, including 70% four- or five-star ratings. Don Norman and Dan Boyarski endorsements are publisher-reproduced, not independent reviews; Mark A. Hart's PDMA review separately supports the historical and practical value. It explains technology development through interviews rather than teaching a technical curriculum. The final process chapter does not override the book's main historical purpose. Transferable design and creative-production principles satisfy H7's explicit exception. Insider testimony requires care about retrospective success stories, but inspected evidence does not establish a serious veto. US-origin computing innovations have global influence; neither thematic deduction applies.
notes: Detailed participant testimony supports development history; retrospective selection limits causal certainty.
Connects hardware, software, human constraints, organizational design and market adoption.
Examples show reusable tradeoffs in prototyping, prioritization and adoption.
Explains constraints behind interface choices, though interviews do not isolate causes experimentally.

D=7.5, moderate confidence from Hart's detailed review, contents and reader reports. Different devices add distinct constraints; long interviews and speculative later sections reduce uniform yield. No full-text density audit.
Development history and design constraints outlast individual products.
Direct fit to computing, technology adoption and creative engineering.
Practitioner with direct design experience and access; favorable specialist reception.
Readable interview-based history, less cumulative than one sustained argument.
Concrete and accessible, with occasional practitioner generalization.
